Incompleteness Theorem linked to physical phenomena. Makes certain physical questions unanswerable
I for one, have always suspected something flawed about the Hamiltonian approximation of the "real" world.

This is interesting, but not really surprising for anyone whom has looked at the nature of knowledge, or how we know things. Fundamental to the act of knowing something about the "real" world, as opposed to ideal models, is the act of experiment. One has to actually try something before it can be considered proven. All concrete and real knowledge is atomic in nature. All facts are axiomatic, in that they are self evident.

If you carry this further, I think this is one of the reasons intelligence has proven such a difficult thing to understand, and especially to replicate. As intelligent beings we use approximations and models all the time, but we always come back to axiomatic fact. Furthermore, we can hold appararently inconsistent axiomatic facts as both being true at the same time because in order to fully understand a system you must first be able to understand it's parts, even in those parts don't fit in a way you've seen before. In simple terms, our brains are wired to be able to feel the elephant's tail and trunk separately before we understand what is in the middle, because even if you never understand the elephant, you can at least understand the trunk and tail, and understanding those is the first step to understanding the elephant as a whole.

As a side note, I'm glad to see this sort of thing being looked at, I've felt like Incompleteness has always been kind of ignored and swept under the rug rather than addressed head-on. While incompleteness is very troubling to some people, I also tend to think it is one of the greatest realizations of human thought, and only serve to strengthen math and inferential thought in general by defining their limits, as well as paving the way for formalized systems of non-inferential logic.

Bohr said that a physicist is an atom's way of thinking about atoms. But if "concept of truth is nonsense" does that mean that the concept of nonsense is true? Or is bullshit irreversible?

Let me elaborate: "truth" simply means that the model is good enough for your purposes. An exact description of something is equal to that thing. I see it as nonsense because you never have a perfect fidelity model. Nothing we say about the real world is "true" in any sense other than it is a model that sufficiently captures what we care about.

For example, Newton's laws are true if you want to build a bridge or fire artillery; relativity if you want to look at Mercury's orbit or keep your GPS from drifting; possibly some undiscovered quantum gravity for more exotic applications; "stuff wants to go back to the earth" if you're a primitive hunter-gatherer society.

The only sort of truth I'll allow is just abstract logic. You can define a formal system and have things that are true to the extent they follow from the rules and axioms of that system. I'd rather just call those theorems than truth though as they have no direct connection to the actual universe.

You can define a formal system and have things that are true to the extent they follow from the rules and axioms of that system.

So the truth of the system you describe does not rest on any foundation, such as physicality, as in the physicalist assertion that "all information is physical"? I guess what I am saying is, if only physical things exist, then in what sense or universe do your axioms exist? A physicalist might claim that once the sentence/axiom "all information is physical" is written down, it consists of physical atoms, and so acquires physical reality and so a kind of truth. Would you say that "F = MA" was true before Newton wrote it down? True because he wrote it down and made it physical? Or just an axiom? I.e. an abstract truth with no relation to anything real such as force or mass. But then do those things not exist? And if they do, why can't you say true things about them?

Now I'll take great care to be very precise. The topic is delicate that way.

Let us first consider another system: a formal analog of number theory. I'll be imagining Hofstadter's TNT from GEB but don't worry if you're not familiar; we're not going to get too specific. After establishing rules and axioms in the formal system for addition and logical operations, you can derive the theorem: 1+1=2. This theorem is correct in that it was properly derived within the formal system. Furthermore, I may say it's true because natural numbers and addition are both good models of how certain physical phenomenon behave. If part of the universe is an apple and I bring another apple part of the universe next to it, this is now two appley bits. I'm pretty comfortable saying that 1+1=2 is true because this is a very good correlation.

So going back to your Newton example, I'd say that it is true only in relation to an intelligence using it with purpose. Any time it's used to create a sufficiently high fidelity model for the purposes of whatever intelligence is doing the modeling, it's true.

Keep in mind too, I don't concede that force and mass are real either. They're also models. Very good models at that. I believe that our entire way of thinking is just built on layer upon layer of correlations. Starting when you're a baby sorting out sensory input flooding in and correlating with each other and real objects in the world, the process continues forever and is inherent in the way we think and communicate. I'd really argue it's what makes us an intelligence: we're little correlation machines.

I guess I can sum it up by saying that I see it as a very weird fusion of Zen and empiricism. I think that truth is impossible to capture with words and thoughts since those are merely models of the monistic universe, but because it is our only way to interact with and understand the universe, we should plough ahead making these empirical models and using them rather than eschewing thoughts, language, and logic.

I think the idea of a mind creating a mental model as layers of correlations makes a great deal of sense. At one point I would have said that the degree to which the model we create correlates with physical reality (or other the models which other people build their minds) is its "truth". But I suspect now that physical reality is so strange that mental models, or at least mine, probably do not correspond to it very well. But as a pluralist I do not think that physicality makes up very much of existence, so if I have a poor model of it, it probably does not matter very much.
